#9611. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

This soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

Okay technically yes, I think you could! But here’s why I prefer not to:

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

– the experience of pouring the broth over the noodles is really fun. 🙂

Any thoughts about using a bone broth / regular broth blend?

Yes, 10 cups! Happens almost every time I make this that I start with 8 cups, thinking it will be enough, and then I always end up adding 2 more (at least) for a total of 10 cups to get the level of brothiness I’m looking for!

Some of it will depend on the thickness of your carrots and celery, so if you aren’t sure you could always start with 8 cups and then add to get your desired final consistency.

#9609. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9608. Fall Freezer Meals #2

These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026

A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.

I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!

And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.

The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!

And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂

Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!

Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.

For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.

Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.

Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.

Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!

Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.

Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.

Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.

Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).

#9607. Underappreciated artists from the Chelsea Hotel are finally getting their due

Bettina standing outside of the Chelsea Hotel, New York Courtesy the artist’s estate

Since its opening in 1884, New York’s Hotel Chelsea has been famed as a hotbed of creativity—a seedy yet alluring beacon drawing artists, musicians and bohemians of all kinds. While the luminaries associated with the place (Mark Twain, Janis Joplin, Andy Warhol) are well known, less famous residents are only now beginning to gain recognition.

Among the more recently “discovered” artists who once called the Chelsea home are the late Bettina (1927-2021), Ching Ho Cheng (1946-89), Bernard Childs (1910-85), Herbert Gentry (1919-2003), Nicola L. (1932-2018) and Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020). Many of their relatives still live in the building; some feel their presence to this day.

“It’s happened many times, Ching contacting me,” Cheng’s sister, Sybao Cheng-Wilson, tells The Art Newspaper. She moved into the Chelsea in the 1980s to take care of her brother, who was dying of Aids. For years after Cheng’s death, the bathroom light bulb would flicker on his birthday, 26 December; Cheng-Wilson became convinced it was his way of checking in on her.

For her part, Cheng-Wilson became dedicated to preserving her brother’s legacy. She held onto both his art and the apartment where he made it. She even raised her daughter at the Chelsea, despite its notorious reputation as a hedonistic haven.

Judith Childs and her artist husband moved into the Chelsea in 1966. “My parents were a little horrified by the whole building,” she recalls. “It was not an elegant hotel.” Childs still lives in the first-floor apartment she and Bernard once shared, surrounded by his soft-hued geometric abstractions that seem to glow from within.

Bernard Childs’s work at the Armory Show 2026 Courtesy Bank

In September, these works—imbued with an almost cosmic fluidity—were the subject of a solo stand at New York’s Armory Show with the Shanghai- and New York-based gallery Bank. The 1970s canvases—priced between $14,000 and $55,000—stood out amid the more than 200 exhibitors at the fair; they hung above a fuzzy, cantaloupe-coloured carpet that enhanced the works’ warm, luminous quality.

Showing an essentially forgotten artist like Childs was a bit of a risk for Bank founder Mathieu Borysevicz. “He’s been off the map for so long,” says the gallerist, who just began working with Childs’s estate. The artist’s work was featured in Documenta in 1959; that same year, he had a solo show at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. But Childs’s previous dealer, Jason McCoy Gallery, last gave the artist an in-person solo show in 2013; the gallery itself closed in 2024.

Borysevicz already had experience helping artists from the storied hotel emerge from the shadows, having worked with the Cheng estate since 2021.

Over Cheng’s short but prolific career, the artist developed four major bodies of work, beginning with psychedelic paintings inspired by Tibetan spiritualism before experimenting with airbrushed gouache, graphite on torn paper and rusted surfaces made using iron and copper oxide on paper. The artist, who appeared in last year’s Sixties Surreal at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art, will have his first major retrospective in September 2027 at the Addison Gallery of American Art in Andover, Massachusetts.

Ching Ho Cheng in his Chelsea Hotel studio in 1985 Courtesy the artist’s estate

Cheng had moved into the Chelsea in 1976, where he befriended Childs. Judith and Cheng-Wilson have stayed close over the years, united by their shared devotion to preserving and promoting their late loved ones’ work. It was Cheng-Wilson who introduced Judith to Borysevicz.

Another friend of Childs, from his time in Paris in the 1950s, was Herbert Gentry—an African American painter known for his jazz-inspired abstractions. He arrived at the hotel in the late 1960s; Gentry’s second wife, the artist Mary Anne Rose, joined him in 1978. She still lives at the Chelsea and now oversees his estate.

“Herbert’s work is so distinctive stylistically, but he was also foundational in bridging what was happening in North America and Europe,” says Gentry’s dealer, Jeffrey Lee of the New York gallery Ryan Lee. By December, the artist will have work simultaneously in museum group shows in Alabama, Germany and Martinique, plus a solo show at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Sweden.

But not all Hotel Chelsea artists have family members on the premises to safeguard their legacies. When the reclusive Bettina died in 2021, management quickly began clearing out her apartment. The unit was nearly bursting with the conceptual artist’s life’s work, to the point where Bettina slept in a lawn chair in the hallway, as memorably captured in the 2022 documentary Dreaming Walls: Inside the Chelsea Hotel. That would have been the end of the story had Bettina not connected with the Moroccan artist Yto Barrada in her final years.

Barrada fervently believed in the value of Bettina’s work, and its need to be saved from the dumpsters and shared with the world. Before Bettina’s death, Barrada presented the older artist’s sculptures at the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council Arts Center on Governors Island, leading to an appearance in Greater New York 2021 at MoMA PS1. When Bettina died, it was Barrada who saved the contents of her apartment from the trash. The estate, which Barrada oversees with the assistance of Anna McCormick-Goodhart, is now represented by Ulrik in New York; a solo show at the Ruth Foundation for the Arts in Milwaukee closed in April.

One of Bettina’s index cards outlining the details of her unrealised exhibition The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work Courtesy the artist’s estate

“There is a lot to sort and sift through, and it leaves wonderful traces of the history of the making of her works, of her travels, of the people in her life—it’s very densely layered,” McCormick-Goodhart says.

In her later years, Bettina—whose work encompasses photography, printmaking, painting, sculpture, textile and commercial design—was known largely for her eccentricities. But she also planned an ambitious, albeit unrealised, exhibition to show her neighbours’ art. A series of typed index cards from the 1980s reveal the artist list and potential venues for The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work. The exhibition would have featured the works of Cheng, Childs, Gentry and Rose, among other residents.

Another artist in this heady milieu was Nicola L. A documentary film-maker, who turned her own lens on her home of nearly 30 years for the 2014 film Doors Ajar at the Chelsea Hotel, Nicola L. is best known for her “functional sculptures”—anthropomorphic furniture shaped like a massive foot, the silhouette of a head and other body parts. In a critique of the objectification of women’s bodies, some mimic the female form, but they somehow avoid feeling overly sexualised.

Nicola L. was largely overlooked until London’s Tate Modern included her work in a broader view of international Pop art for its 2015 exhibition The World Goes Pop. Nicola L.’s first institutional solo show took place in 2017 at New York’s SculptureCenter; the London gallery Alison Jacques began representing her estate after the artist’s death in 2018. A retrospective, When the Earth Turned the Other Way, closed earlier this month at Belgium’s Museum of Contemporary Art in Antwerp, and the travelling museum show I Am the Last Woman Object wrapped up a European tour in March.

Installation view of Nicola L.: When the Earth Turned the Other Way, Museum of Contemporary Art, Antwerp, Belgium Courtesy Alison Jacques

Nicola L. was the catalyst behind the Chelsea Hotel residents’ successful fight to keep their apartments after new ownership embarked on an 11-year renovation project to transform the property into a high-end hotel—where rates start at around $500 per night. It was at her urging that the residents banded together to successfully protect their rent-stabilised tenancy.

“The Chelsea was a safe haven for these artists,” says Christophe Lanzenberg, Nicola L.’s son. “The Chelsea allowed them to thrive and stay in New York, instead of getting kicked out of places where rents were coming up.”

Today, there are 42 families still living at the Chelsea. (One artist, Gerald DeCock, is facing eviction at the end of February after 31 years in residence.) Over the years, those remaining have forged tight bonds.

When Childs died, Gentry sent Rose downstairs to keep Judith company. Rose and Nicola L. shared a Long Island City studio for years. As Nicola L.’s health began to decline due to Alzheimer’s, Rose and Judith kept a close watch. They let her sons know when their mother could no longer live alone.

Though its heyday as a refuge for free-spirited artists is long past, the hotel is still deeply connected to its creative history, including artists who checked out decades ago. The lobby, stairwells and hallways are filled with works of art, some said to have been given to the longtime manager Stanley Bard (1934-2017) in lieu of rent. A new Japanese restaurant, Teruko, opened in the basement last year featuring paintings by its namesake, Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020), who lived at the Chelsea from 1957 to 1960, during her marriage to Sam Francis (1923-94).

Teruko Yokoi’s Untitled (1959) will be on offer on Hollis Taggart’s stand at New York’s ADAA Fair in November Courtesy Hollis Taggart

“I was a baby when she was just coming out of art school, juggling having a newborn and continuing to paint. Her studio was actually in the apartment,” says Yokoi’s daughter, Kayo Malik, who is also a custodian of her estate. But when the couple hosted parties for friends like Mark Rothko and Al Leslie, Francis would have Yokoi put her paintings away, hiding her work.

At the Teruko restaurant, the artist’s pieces are displayed in the dining room, enjoyed and appreciated by guests gathering to share a meal—“a full circle moment”, Malik says. The artist is also the subject of a solo show, Seasons, at New York’s Hollis Taggart (until 25 November). And the gallery is bringing one of Yokoi’s Hotel Chelsea-era works, Untitled (1959), to the ADAA Fair at New York’s Park Avenue Armory (12-16 November); there, it will be on offer at a two-person presentation with the artist Michael West (1908-91). Meanwhile in Los Angeles, the artist has a solo show currently on view at James Fuentes Gallery (until 7 November).

Yokoi eventually moved to Switzerland after separating from Francis. Determined to show her work, she opened two dedicated museums in her native Japan, enjoying a long career across three continents. But Malik still feels close ties to her first home at the Chelsea, that formative chapter in Yokoi’s life, and its vibrant artist community.

“The hotel has had an incredible life,” Malik says.

The influence of New York on the Greek-born artist informs an exhibition designed to fill in the gaps of her story

The five-gallery fair was staged inside one of Manhattan's most famous hotels

The artist’s former residence opens a restaurant named Teruko this month, featuring her works

As a survey on the US artist opens at Tate Modern, there is no shortage of works inspired by his "Combines" at the fair

#9605. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

[Get This Free Download: Learn How Hormones Impact ADHD Symptoms]

When estrogen and progesterone rise in girls, ADHD symptoms fluctuate. Here’s how:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

Girls who menstruate may also experience pronounced changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle.

Girls who mature early may feel distressed when their physical development outpaces their cognitive, emotional, and social development.

[Read: The Menstrual Cycle Impacts ADHD Symptoms in Disparate Ways]

“I can’t control the wind, but I can adjust my sails.”

“I can notice this moment without judging it.”

What activity could give my mind a break?

“I can choose where to place my attention.”

Molly Nikolas, Ph.D., is an associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Iowa.

#9604. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

Many of the factors known to contribute to burnout are systemic and need to be addressed by health care organizations.2 However, physicians can take action to limit their stress and prevent exhaustion. The following strategies may help mitigate burnout2,4,13:

#9603. New Perinatal Guidance for Women with ADHD

ADHD medication should not be reflexively stopped during pregnancy or breastfeeding, according to new research.

During pregnancy and the post-partum period, hormonal fluctuations and mounting demands on executive function intensify ADHD symptoms. Poor memory, dysregulated emotions, and disrupted sleep become elevated (and exhausting) during an already-stressful time.

Paradoxically, the vast majority of pregnant women with ADHD stop treating the condition with medication on the advice of their healthcare providers. Patients have been historically told to cease using stimulant and non-stimulant medication during pregnancy due to a lack of safety data and fear of potential risks to the fetus. But new research has produced generally reassuring reproductive safety data — and pushed more providers to weigh risks on both sides of the treatment equation.

How might untreated ADHD impact a woman’s mental health and her ability to manage the extraordinary demands of caring for an infant? Could ceasing treatment pose a bigger risk to the fetus than continuing it? What are the dangers associated with abruptly stopping treatment without monitoring, support, or a plan? These questions deserve to be asked.

Not every woman should continue medication, but neither should every woman stop. This decision should account for symptom severity, individual history, co-occurring conditions, gestational risks, and the consequences of untreated ADHD. These factors should be discussed with a medical team over multiple visits.

Use these recommendations — adapted in part from guidelines published in the American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology — to begin conversations with your medical team about your health and your baby’s health.

[Read: We Demand Attention on the Safety and Efficacy of ADHD Medication Use During Pregnancy]

If you take a stimulant, talk with your prescriber about whether a supervised trial without medication is appropriate. Discontinuation may be reasonable for some women with mild ADHD who function well with non-pharmacological supports.

[Read: ADHD Meds Should Not Be “Panic Stopped” in Pregnancy]

It is reasonable to continue stimulant treatment if it is required for daily functioning. Discuss these options with your doctor:

Most studies have shown no adverse effects among infants exposed to maternal ADHD medications. Amphetamines may increase the risk of preeclampsia and other adverse gestational outcomes, but the absolute risk appears low. Meanwhile, studies show that discontinuing medication during pregnancy may worsen ADHD symptoms, mental health, and daily functioning.

Medication decisions should consider the risks associated with a fetus’ medication exposure and those associated with untreated ADHD. Some women choose to limit or stop medication during pregnancy and optimize treatment after delivery. If stimulant use is a concern, ask about lowering the dose, using medication intermittently, or considering another treatment.

Regular care allows your clinician to monitor fetal growth as well as your blood pressure, weight, and other health measures that may be affected by stimulant use.

Work with your care team to anticipate changes in symptoms, sleep, and mood in the postpartum period — a sensitive time when you may need greater support. Your proactive plan might include:

Inattention, emotional dysregulation, and executive dysfunction intensify in the postpartum period. Women with ADHD face a substantially greater risk of postpartum mood and anxiety symptoms.

Allison S. Baker, M.D., is a clinician, researcher, and educator with the Perinatal and Reproductive Psychiatry Clinical Research Program at Massachusetts General Hospital.

#9602. Easy Jalapeño Corn Fritters (Vegan)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Just when we thought summer’s most perfect veggie couldn’t get any more delicious, corn FRITTERS graced our palettes. These crispy-on-the-outside, tender-on-the-inside, lightly spiced fritters are a must-try appetizer or side!

Not only are they incredibly delicious, but these fritters are vegan, optionally gluten-free, and SO easy to make! Grab your mixing bowl and 10 basic ingredients, and you’ll be enjoying fritters in 30 minutes or less. What are you waiting for? Let’s do this, friends!

Giving traditional corn fritters a vegan spin requires a couple adjustments. First, instead of eggs for binding, we rely on flaxseed meal. And instead of milk, we rely on a neutral-flavored, unsweetened dairy-free milk (homemade cashew being our favorite). The rest of the ingredients are pretty classic, but we gave these fritters our own flavor spin and also made them gluten-free!

Besides flaxseed meal and dairy-free milk, the ingredients for the batter include baking powder for fluffiness; salt, garlic powder, and nutritional yeast for flavor; and all-purpose flour or gluten-free blend to thicken it.

You’re looking for a thick, fluffy batter, which can be achieved by adding more flour or dairy-free milk as needed. With the batter ready, we’re just 3 ingredients away from fritter time!

Next up, fresh corn gets nestled into the chunky batter, along with finely chopped jalapeño for a subtle heat. While we love using fresh ingredients when it’s summertime, this recipe also works with frozen corn — just let it thaw at room temperature, then pat dry with paper towels to remove extra moisture. And if you don’t have fresh jalapeño, a pinch of cayenne would likely work as well!

Now for the frying! Instead of deep frying, we go with a shallow fry, cooking for 2-3 minutes per side in avocado oil in a cast iron skillet. Not only do we find shallow frying less daunting, but it minimizes the amount of oil needed and maximizes the health benefits. Win, win, win! And still, major YUM!

When the fritters are golden on both sides, it’s time to enjoy! They’re incredibly flavorful on their own (we were snacking right off the cooling rack), but they’re also amazing paired with a sauce. Try our Go-To Guacamole, Creamy Cashew Jalapeño Sauce, or Easy Vegan Ranch Dressing.

We hope you LOVE these corn fritters, friends! They’re:SavoryCrispyNaturally a little sweetJust a little spicyQuick & easy& SO delicious!

This is the perfect appetizer or side to make during peak summer, when fresh corn and jalapeños are in season! However, they’re so delicious you may find yourself craving them year-round (in which case, using frozen corn is also a great option).

These fritters are flavorful without being heavily seasoned, making them a good fit for pairing with a variety of other sides and mains, especially grilled proteins, side salads, and anything BBQ seasoned (hello, summertime!). Here are several delicious pairings:

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9600. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9597. Perimenopause Begins Earlier and Hits Harder for Women with ADHD

Women with ADHD may experience more severe perimenopause symptoms, and at younger ages. Learn how to recognize the signs and find relief.

Perimenopause is destabilizing, and even debilitating for many women with ADHD. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 5,000 women, 63% of respondents aged 45 and older said ADHD had the greatest impact on their lives during the menopausal transition.

Fluctuating estrogen levels affect attention, memory, executive function, and emotional regulation. Meanwhile, hot flashes, poor sleep, anxiety, and brain fog place added stress on an already strained nervous system.

Emerging research suggests that women with ADHD may experience perimenopause and its symptoms earlier than their neurotypical peers. In a study published in European Psychiatry, women with ADHD reported their most severe perimenopausal symptoms from ages 35 to 39 — almost a decade younger than women without ADHD. Their symptoms were also relatively more severe, which may help explain the uptick in ADHD diagnoses at this time.1

We cannot yet definitively say that hormonal changes begin earlier in women with ADHD. However, research suggests that significant symptoms of perimenopause may emerge earlier than clinicians expect.

If your periods, sleep, mood, or ADHD symptoms have changed, do not dismiss them because a doctor says you’re “too young” for menopause. These changes deserve thoughtful medical evaluation.

[Free Webinar Replay: Perimenopause in Women with ADHD]

In a large study published in the journal Menopause, one in three women aged 35 and older said they were unsure whether they were in perimenopause. Many did not know whether their symptoms reflected hormonal changes, especially if their periods remained regular and/or they had other health conditions. About 16% attributed their uncertainty to barriers such as dismissive healthcare encounters, including being told they were “too young.” 2

Uncertainty was highest among women with the most severe symptoms. Put another way, the women who might benefit most from intervention were the least likely to know they were in perimenopause.

Adding to the problem, some women experience perimenopause symptoms while their menstrual cycles remain regular. They may not develop obvious menstrual changes until later in the transition or until they’ve entered menopause.

“It is a universal transition with ambiguity and often lack of validation,” the study’s authors wrote. Better symptom recognition and communication are critical first steps toward improving care.

Use the Perimenopause Log below to identify patterns and track physical symptoms and symptoms related to mood, menstrual cycle, ADHD, cognition, and ADHD medication efficacy. Keep a journal to record more specific experiences, such as missing an appointment, losing words during a conversation, or forgetting to complete tasks that once seemed manageable.

Hormone tests are typically used when symptoms begin earlier than expected, the diagnosis is unclear, or another condition is suspected. If testing is warranted, your doctor should look at follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and estrogen levels. FSH signals the ovaries to develop eggs and produce estradiol. As ovarian function becomes less predictable during perimenopause, FSH generally rises to compensate while estradiol fluctuates. Multiple tests may be needed to establish a clear picture.

If you are younger than 40 and have irregular periods along with perimenopause symptoms, ask whether you should be evaluated for primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), a condition that requires careful treatment.

I use the term “hormone stabilization therapy,” or HST, to describe hormonal treatment during perimenopause, when the goal is to smooth disruptive hormonal swings rather than replace hormones after menstruation has ended.

Certainty that you are in perimenopause is not required before discussing relief. Treatment should focus on the symptoms causing the greatest problems even while your doctor continues to evaluate their source.

Estrogen therapy relieves symptoms of perimenopause and may improve the effectiveness of ADHD stimulant medication. Prior use of estrogen therapy may render it less effective. If you have a uterus and use systemic estrogen, you will need a progestogen to protect the uterine lining. The type and schedule should be individualized. Vaginal estrogen may be an option for urinary or vaginal symptoms, including for some women who cannot use systemic treatment.

ADHD medication may need to change — whether it’s the dose, timing, or type of medication — during this stage for continued symptom control.

Birth control is often recommended for its role in smoothing hormonal fluctuations. In my clinical experience, progestin-only birth control may worsen mood and symptoms of ADHD in some women Talk to your provider about your symptoms and whether other birth control options may be right for you.

Antidepressants and other non-hormonal medications can help manage hot flashes, mood swings, anxiety, and depression.

Keep track of your results. When possible, make one planned change at a time so it will be easier to understand what has helped.

Women with ADHD need support during perimenopause. Take your needs seriously and seek counseling, ADHD coaching, or peer-support groups to help you find new ways to cope.

Patricia O. Quinn, M.D., is a developmental pediatrician and international authority on ADHD.

#9596. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9595. Psychiatry ICD-10 Codes

This is a comprehensive table of psychiatry ICD 10 codes used by researchers and healthcare professionals and personnel – nurses, medical coders, physicians, et al. This table has been curated for psychiatrists and mental health specialists to include all psychiatry ICD 10 codes and classifications relevant to psychiatric and mental health conditions.

The World Health Organization originally authorized the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) for mortality coding and classification from United States death certificates. A Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) was developed for medical diagnoses, and a Procedure Coding System (ICD-10-PCS) was used to classify inpatient procedures. Psychiatry ICD-10 codes in the ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS replace and update psychiatry ICD codes in all three volumes of the ICD-9-CM.

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9594. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

#9593. The Ongoing Crisis in Menopause Care

Few medical providers are adequately trained to treat menopause, a new study finds, and even fewer understand how hormonal changes aggravate ADHD symptoms.

Suffering through menopausal hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood shifts, and memory problems? Wondering why your ADHD medication has suddenly become less effective? Considering a visit with your doctor to better understand and treat these deeply disruptive symptoms?

Sadly, your healthcare provider may be less informed than you might hope.

A disturbing but unsurprising analysis, published recently in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health, found that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate this often-challenging stage of life. It cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”1

The analysis of 89 studies on health system responsiveness across the U.S. and several other countries also found that women in marginalized groups disproportionately experienced barriers to care and received limited information about available treatment options by providers.

A woman who has gone 12 months without a menstrual period is in menopause. The median age for menopause is 51, though many women with ADHD are known to experience the onset earlier.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

Declining estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause are associated with reduced dopamine, leading to worsening ADHD symptoms and emotional dysregulation in many women – even those who had previously managed their ADHD symptoms well with medication, according to a separate study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.

In surveys conducted over recent years, thousands of women have disclosed to ADDitude how midlife hormonal changes exacerbated their ADHD symptoms and adversely affected every area of their lives, from work performance and sleep to relationships with family and friends. Many said they sought help from providers who had limited knowledge and few clinical studies to consult.

“Perimenopause and menopause play a big role in my inattentive ADHD, and I wish more was known by those who diagnose and treat us,” said Cindy, a ADDitude reader from Santa Clara, California.

“The fact that females are massively underdiagnosed and understudies is horrible but not surprising,” said another ADDitude reader who was diagnosed with ADHD at age 38. “How symptoms may change during perimenopause and menopause, how this affects your home life as a wife and mother, is not talked about enough.”

“It’s insane,” said another ADDitude reader, “and nobody is helping us to treat the super storm of symptoms, including brain fog, exhaustion, headaches, and so on.”

Menopausal hormone therapy is considered the most effective treatment for alleviating common symptoms and is often recommended for women experiencing adverse effects of perimenopause. Non-hormonal medications and complementary approaches, including cognitive behavioral therapy, have also shown benefits in symptom management, the Lancet analysis said.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

#9592. Celebrated photographer Pipo Nguyen-duy and his wife murdered by his son, according to police

Pipo Nguyen-duy, a celebrated photographer and a monumental figure on a small campus in rural Ohio, has died, aged 64. Authorities found Nguyen-duy and his wife Tran Thi Phong dead from gunshot wounds in their home in Oberlin, Ohio, on 28 October. One of Nguyen-duy’s two sons, Daniel Jones (also known as Asia Nguyen-duy), was taken into custody that same day and has been charged with six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence.

Nguyen-duy arrived in the US at the age of 13 as a refugee from Vietnam, where he once competed in national table tennis championships. He briefly lived in India as a Buddhist monk before graduating from Carleton College in Minnesota with a degree in economics. He then worked in New York nightlife for several years before earning Master of Arts and Master of Fine Arts degrees from the University of New Mexico in Albuquerque.

His practice often dealt with themes of immigration, colonialism, Orientalism, and identity, as he used both contemporary and historic photographic methods to navigate the implications of living in a country whose military incursion had made him a refugee in the first place. He was also interested in performance, both in terms of its relationship to photography and as professional practice (for a 2001 project, he played table tennis against a machine in a hotel room for three hours).

In 1998 he moved to Ohio and became a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College. At the time of his death he had been serving a two-year tenure as the chair of the college’s art department, having postponed his retirement on more than one occasion due to his commitment to his students.

Nguyen-duy was skilled at historic practices, including tintypes and large-format photography, which was how I began studying under him as an undergraduate visual art student, alongside classmates and artists including Gregory Wikstrom, Erika Råberg, Lex Voight and Sam Draisin. Draisin once volunteered to drive Nguyen-duy’s Guggenheim Fellowship application from Oberlin to New York in 2010 to hand-deliver it to the committee after he had missed the mailing deadline. He received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2011, becoming one of the few Vietnamese artists to do so.

Pipo Nguyen-duy, Untitled (AnOther Western), 1998 Courtesy of CLAMP, New York

In addition to the Guggenheim Fellowship, Nguyen-duy was a recipient of the the Lila Wallace-Reader’s Digest Artists at Giverny Fellowship, which allowed him to live and work in Claude Monet’s garden in Giverny, France, where he created the AnOther Expedition series of cyanotype photographs, one of his most widely exhibited bodies of work. He was also the recipient of a National Endowment for the Arts grant, an En Foco Grant, a professional development grant from the College Arts Association, a national graduate fellowship from the American Photography Institute, a fellowship from the Oregon Arts Commission, a B. Wade and Jane B. White Fellowship in the Humanities at Oberlin College and three individual artist fellowships from the Ohio Arts Council.

Nguyen-duy would insist on teaching all dimensions of photography, from the dark room to obscure historic processes to building frames in the woodshop, training his students to be self-reliant and capable of telling their stories unimpeded by technical limitations or logistics. In order to work in the photography studio as a lab monitor, a hallowed position, he would put students through a very simple test to determine their capacity to colour-calibrate the monitors, a test many of us considered a rite of passage.

“Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography, and I know that many of you are familiar with Pipo and his artistry,” Carmen Twillie Ambar, the president of Oberlin College, wrote in a letter to students, faculty, staff and alumni on 29 October. She invited recipients to participate in a digital forum of remembrance, which has since gathered dozens of tributes.

“Pipo to me is more than a professor. He is a dear friend, a mentor, a role model I look up to dearly,” wrote Loan Lu, who graduated from Oberlin in 2015. “He has a contagious energy that brightens every room he walks into, light up every person he speaks to. He is wise, humble, full of love for life, he is all I want to be when I grow older. We had promised each other to hang out in Vietnam when he retires, and I have been looking forward to that day so much.”

Another student only identified as Seth, a graduate from 2004, praised his former professor: “Pipo is on a very short list of educators who have most profoundly impacted my life. I struggled with traditional academia and longed for something to do with my hands. I longed to learn techniques, new and archaic. Pipo was a breath of fresh air. His experimental photography course was foundational to the path my life has taken. He taught me to make magic out of light and a few chemicals. He taught me how to see beauty and wonder in the most rundown and weary settings.”

Nguyen-duy is represented by the ClampArt gallery in New York.

#9584. Works from US pavilion at Venice Biennale could be stuck in limbo due to fundraising shortfall

Installation view of Alma Allen’s Call Me the Breeze at the US Pavilion, Venice BIennale 2026 Photo: © Agostino Osio, Alto Piano Studio, courtesy Perrotin

With a little less than a month left of this year’s Venice Biennale, the US pavilion is in the news again—this time not for aesthetic but financial reasons. According to Zachary Small of The New York Times, the non-profit responsible for the pavilion has sounded the alarm that it needs to raise $1m or it will not be able to ship Alma Allen’s hulking sculptures back to the US.

“We are facing an urgent funding need associated with the final deinstallation and safe return of the artworks to the United States,” Jenni Parido, the director of the American Arts Conservancy (AAC), wrote in a plea to donors. She added that the organisation had only been able to raise $1.4m out of the $2.5m total needed for the pavilion.

While the State Department provided its usual $375,000 grant for the US pavilion this year, the rest was left up to Parido—a former pet-store owner with little background in art outside of a degree in graphic design—and her brand-new non-profit to raise. (Parido is a friend of the director of the State Department’s Art in Embassies programme, Erin Scavino—a former contestant on Donald Trump’s television programme The Apprentice.)

The funding shortfall comes even as this year’s US pavilion was lauded for costing much less money than usual. (The 2024 pavilion's budget was $5m, and in 2022 the pavilion cost $7m.) The AAC did most of its fundraising via private events with donors including the fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger and the art collector (and former US Navy secretary) John Phelan.

“Budgeting normally is very careful,” Katy Siegel, an art historian who co-curated the 2017 US Pavilion, told the Times. “Maybe there is no oversight now. This is crazy.” She added that finding space in Venice to store Allen’s sculptures—some of which weigh almost a ton—would be very difficult.

As for the Mexico-based Allen, he told the Times that he was unaware of the AAC’s financial woes. “I received only reimbursement for travel and my Airbnb,” he said, “which was cheap.”

#9581. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9578. Art Toronto reflects Canadian art community’s focus on sustaining domestic ecosystem

Lynn Donoghue's Untitled (Watching) (1996) at Art Toronto Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is something strangely comforting about this year’s edition of Art Toronto (until 1 November), Canada’s biggest art fair. In spite of the vast 20,000 sq. ft of space it inhabits at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, there is a sense of warmth and grounding in Canadian landscapes made manifest in the installation that welcomes visitors to the art fair’s 27th iteration: Untitled (Watching) (1996) by the late Lynn Donoghue and the first of her Caribou Tarp series to be shown in public, installed here on top of a pile of dirt.

Inspired by the artist’s time in Alberta in the mid 1990s, when she encountered discarded caribou antlers scattered across the tundra, the work speaks to one of the overarching themes at the fair this year, of a return to natural roots. But this Art Toronto is also about uniting the often-scattered Canadian art landscape and, as per the title of one series of talks at the fair, “Building a Stronger Arts Ecosystem”.

These are trying times for Canadian artists and galleries, hammered by a trade war with the US and larger macro-economic forces such as inflation, war and related fuel costs. Happily, though the fair’s new director Emily Jean Alexander tells The Art Newspaper that this year’s Art Toronto is “only down in capacity by 5%”, while some other international art fairs have pared back their exhibitor numbers more drastically. She says there are far fewer US galleries this year than in past editions, while 80% of the 105 exhibitors are Canadian. A commercial gallery from New Brunswick is participating for the first time, alongside dozens from British Columbia, Québec and Ontario. There is a pervasive tariffs-be-damned, “elbows up” sense of artistic solidarity afoot and, Alexander says, a renewed commitment to creating a sustainable art market in Canada.

Rich Loen's Databells (2025) at Art Toronto, presented in partnership with Artist Project Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is a nostalgic, McLuhanesque installation on the convention centre’s ground floor (presented with Art Toronto’s sister fair, Artist Project) by the Ottawa-based former software engineer Rich Loen. Titled Databells (2025), it connects a collection of bells with statistics ranging from the whimsical (the number of female orgasms per minute) to the digital (the number of TikTok videos played globally per minute) to the serious (amount of carbon dioxide removed from the earth’s atmosphere). The installation’s church and door bells chime at numerically precise intervals, creating a balm for our information-overloaded minds and sparking a meditative state akin to a Balinese temple. It is the perfect hybrid analogue-digital cleanse before the throng of Art Toronto’s main floor.

As visitors ascend into the fair, they can contemplate Kathy Slade’s monumental tapestry Sinking in the West (2023), presented by Mónica Reyes Gallery, which considers recurrence, time and landscape. Turning the corner, visitors will find the McMichael Canadian Art Collection stand; the Kleinburg, Ontario-based museum is currently closed for an expansion and renovation. At the fair it is showing off a recent acquisition, My First Medicine Teacher, a large-scale painting by the Métis artist Christi Belcourt.

A view of Art Toronto including, at centre, the McMichael Canadian Art Collection's stand with My First Medicine Teacher by Christi Belcour Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

Nearby, the Toronto-based Nicholas Metivier Gallery has two stands: one featuring a selection of works by gallery artists, the other showcasing four decades of work by the Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky. The solo stand includes two new photographs from the artist’s forthcoming project, Mining: For the Future. Burtynsky tells The Art Newspaper that he got his start in aerial photography in Western Australia two decades ago and he returned there last year to revisit a subject he has explored since the mid 1980s. The textural, painterly images in vibrant colours reveal both the brutality and beauty of mining materials such as lithium, copper and cobalt that are needed for components in the technologies that will enable a more sustainable future.

Another highlight of the fair, on the stand of Montreal’s Galerie Nicolas Robert, is Ascension (for Bakers) by the artist Sameer Farooq. An extension of his ongoing Flatbread Library, a long-term research project centred on the political and social significance of the tandoor, the new work connects the forms of collected bakeware with the Buddhist stupa reliquary. The appetising installation features a gathering of vessels, bread forms and tools that honour bakers as sculptors, tracing how ideas, objects and food move across cultures.

Next to it is the Vancouver-based gallery Wil Aballe, whose stand includes a work that has been attracting curatorial interest: Karin Jones’s The Bond (dress) (2023) is a mixed-media take on Queen Victoria’s wedding gown re-imagined with blonde hair extensions as a brilliant expression of the politics of adornment and beauty within contemporary material culture.

Additional eye-catching installations at the fair include Douglas Scholes’s (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024), a large-scale sculpture made from beeswax (presented by Galerie Robertson Arès), and the Montréal-based artist Karine Giboulo’s whimsical environment Joy is a Resistant Bacteria (The Living Room) (2026), presented by Art Mûr. Taken together, they convey a sense of the power of the organic overcoming the antiseptic aesthetics of the digital.

Douglas Scholes's (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024) at Art Toronto, presented by Galerie Robertson Arès Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

The booth of Toronto’s Nia Centre for the Arts, Canada’s first professional Black arts centre, features the wonderful painting Califia by the Congolese Canadian artist Heritier Bilaka, paying homage to the warrior Queen Nzinga. (Concurrently with Art Toronto, Nia is hosting A Black Art Fair at its headquarters on Oakwood Avenue.)

The Vancouver-based gallery Ceremonial Art is showing works by five artists on its booth, including a remarkable woodblock print by the Tofino-based artist Marika Swan. Titled Embraced in Interdependence, it is both a rare example of West Coast Indigenous art in Toronto and a neat metaphor for the current socio-political climate in Canada and at the art fair.

A nearby stand is devoted to Portfolio, a nonprofit run by a collective of Vancouver artists and dedicated to helping emerging artists via scholarships funded from a percentage of their sales. Among others, the organisation is showing new paintings by Angela Grossman and new works from the Predator series by Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun—who will open a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Ontario in February 2027.

A few booths away, Vancouver’s Equinox Gallery is showing early paintings by the late artist Gathie Falk, mid-century prints from the Fred Herzog archive and a work by Sonny Assu that playfully subverts the colonial landscapes of Emily Carr by overlaying them with Kwakwaka'wakw formline designs.

During the fair’s gala preview on Thursday (29 October), benefiting the McMichael Canadian Art Collection, it was revealed that the federal and provincial governments would provide C$50m ($35.7m) each in funding for the renovation of the existing building and construction of a new wing, all designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects. In a video marking the occasion, Canada’s first lady, Diana Fox Carney, proclaimed: “The world needs more Canada.” At this year’s Art Toronto, there is plenty to go around.
