#9577. Ozempic may have revealed the brain’s hidden “craving center”

For many people, the thought of a tasty burger or a cold pint of beer conjures up a vivid mental image and drives behavior.

This link between thinking and doing serves a clear function – it motivates us to get the necessities for life.

But for some, this process can malfunction. Preoccupation with these rewarding stimuli can lead to disorders of substance overuse, including overeating to the point of obesity and alcohol abuse.

Studies going back to the 1970s have linked vivid mental imagery with drug abuse.

Understanding this link between craving and consuming is central to understanding addiction. This has eluded neuroscience for decades, but the introduction of a new class of drugs for weight loss may have given us just the lever we need to understand it.

These new drugs – including Ozempic and Wegovy – mimic the GLP-1 hormone to stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and increase feelings of fullness. They are known as GLP-1 agonists and were originally used to treat type 2 diabetes because they help control blood sugar.

As a side effect, people using these drugs also lost a lot of weight, in some cases almost as much as might be expected from bariatric surgery.

But there is another less well publicised effect. Human studies show that GLP-1 agonists reduce alcohol consumption. Preclinical animal studies suggest these drugs also reduce the use of cocaine, amphetamines, opiates and nicotine.

These drugs are changing how we think about the brain’s reward system. They may also open new treatment options for obesity, alcohol dependence and the consumption of other addictive substances.

We have a reasonable understanding of the brain’s “reward circuitry” associated with regions that produce the neurotransmitter dopamine.

These brain parts – the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) – have been the subject of research on reward for decades. They are the obvious candidate regions to look for a mechanism for GLP-1 action in the brain. But they lack significant density of receptors for GLP-1 and are unlikely to be the direct mechanism.

We must, therefore, consider other brain regions to understand the anti-consumption effect of GLP-1 drugs.

One jump “upstream” from the dopamine-producing brain parts is a region called the lateral septum. This brain structure has been historically implicated in emotional regulation.

Back in 1953, pioneering US behavioural researchers Joseph Brady and Walle Nauta coined the term “septal rage” when animals with damage in the lateral septum showed increased aggression, while direct stimulation of this brain region reduced aggression.

Much more recent work has placed the lateral septum at the center of a neural connectivity network. This has reframed how we think about its function.

While a link between the lateral septum and another region called the hypothalamus is probably responsible for septal rage, the lateral septum links with many other regions with various functions.

The lateral septum inherits much of its primary input from a brain region called the hippocampus.

This region is well known as the place that lets us form long-term “episodic memories.” A famous case of hippocampal damage, Henry Molaison (patient HM), was unable to form new memories after his surgery for epilepsy. He effectively lived without a past, in permanent present tense.

The hippocampus also contains the remarkable “place cells” – neurons that fire corresponding to a person’s thoughts about their position in space and, as recent research has shown, time.

This “where and when am I” information gets forwarded to the lateral septum. Key research has recently shown the lateral septum also contains place cells, but these cells strongly respond to rewards. They effectively add “what is good in this place” to the “where and when am I” information from the hippocampus.

Critically, the lateral septum shares this information with the dopamine-producing regions we would normally associate with reward.

Neuroscientists now think of the lateral septum as the brain region that lets us “think about” rewards – our conscious perception of them – and communicates with the machinery in the brain’s reward system that produces dopamine to make us feel good about them.

There is one last reason to suspect the lateral septum as the mechanism behind the anti-consumption effect of GLP-1 agonists. It is absolutely loaded with GLP-1 receptors.

Emerging research points to this as the mechanism. GLP-1 activation directly in the lateral septum has recently been shown to reduce food consumption in mice. Earlier this year, another study showed the same for alcohol consumption.

My own lab has shown this year that GLP-1 drugs reduce a type of activity in the lateral septum that may prevent it communicating so effectively with other brain regions.

These findings are reshaping our understanding of how the brain processes rewards and have put the spotlight firmly on the lateral septum as the home of cravings.

#9576. Does ADHD Worsen With Age? It Depends.

Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first became meaningful to how sensitive one’s ADHD is to their environment.

Not too long ago, ADHD was largely thought of as a childhood condition that diminished in adulthood. Today, we understand that ADHD is a lifelong condition. What’s less clear: How does ADHD change across the lifespan, if at all?

This is a question that professor and clinical psychologist Margaret Sibley, Ph.D., addressed during her ADDitude webinar, “How ADHD Symptoms & Impairments Change with Age.”

The answer is still coming into focus but one central truth is emerging: There isn’t a single ADHD experience. Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first become meaningful to how sensitive the individual’s ADHD is to their environment.

Sibley’s take-home from the research? “It depends on who you are.”

The question of how ADHD changes over time — whether it gets better or worse for people — is tricky, in part, because of the symptom vs. impairment question. That is, someone may show symptoms of ADHD, but the degree to which those symptoms impact their life may shift with age, overall health, and myriad other circumstances.

[Your Free Guide to ADHD in Older Adults]

“Not everyone who has symptoms is impaired,” Sibley said.

From major life transitions (like perimenopause and its accompanying impacts on cognition), environmental demands (e.g., a job that strains executive functioning) to coping skills, what’s going on in someone’s life “may influence whether a person actually experiences problems because of their symptoms,” Sibley said.

The question of whether ADHD worsens or improves over time suggests that the condition is linear. For many people, this is not the case.

“It doesn’t get better or get worse. But depending on what’s happening in your life, you may have good years and not-good years,” Sibley said, whose research found that higher environmental demands are associated with “better-functioning ADHD.”

[Read: ADHD’s Vanishing and Reappearing Act]

If you’ve experienced symptoms and impairments since childhood, your symptoms will likely get better, while impairments may or may not worsen.

If your symptoms first began to impact you in adulthood — perhaps triggered by aging, hormonal fluctuations, or other changes — research suggests that your symptoms and impairments may worsen over time.

If you’re part of the subgroup of people whose ADHD fluctuates from year to year, you may have a form of ADHD that is environmentally sensitive.

#9575. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9574. Scientists discover a hidden brain rhythm that could improve Parkinson’s treatment

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can reduce movement problems caused by Parkinson's disease, and new research is providing a clearer picture of why the treatment works. Scientists have found that its benefits appear to depend on stimulating a specific brain network that communicates primarily through a relatively fast beta rhythm (20 to 35 Hz).

The findings come from an interdisciplinary group of neuroscientists and clinicians at the University Hospitals of Cologne and Düsseldorf, Harvard Medical School and Charité Berlin. Published in the journal Brain, the study, 'The Deep Brain Stimulation Response Network in Parkinson's Disease Operates in the High Beta Band', is the first to bring together two approaches that have largely been studied separately: electrophysiology and brain imaging.

Pinpointing Where and How Brain Stimulation Works

"For the first time, we were able to characterize the DBS response network in Parkinson's disease in terms of space and time, simultaneously," says Professor Dr. Andreas Horn from the University of Cologne, who led the study and specializes in computational neurology. "We show that Parkinson's disease can best be treated if we stimulate a very precisely defined network. This network operates synchronized within a specific frequency band, and offers an explanation for how well patients respond to deep brain stimulation."

Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus is already an established therapy for easing motor symptoms in people with Parkinson's disease. The treatment uses implanted electrodes to deliver small electrical pulses to areas located deep inside the brain.

Previous research has provided only part of the picture. Brain imaging studies have helped identify the locations where stimulation appears to work most effectively, while electrophysiological research has measured the frequencies of the electrical signals involved. Until now, researchers had not captured both the spatial location and timing of these signals at the same time.

To investigate this connection, the team studied a large multicenter group consisting of fifty patients and one hundred brain hemispheres. The scientists simultaneously recorded brain activity through the implanted DBS electrodes and with magnetoencephalography (MEG).

Using these recordings, they mapped functional connections between regions deep within the brain and areas closer to its surface.

Their analysis revealed that the important network connecting the subthalamic nucleus with frontal areas of the brain communicates largely at a comparatively fast frequency (20-35 Hz). Importantly, the strength of this connection was associated with how much individual patients' motor symptoms improved following electrode implantation.

A Brain Rhythm That May Shape Treatment Response

"These results suggest that a certain rhythm of the brain acts as a communication channel between the subthalamic nucleus and the cerebral cortex and may mediate the therapeutic effects of deep brain stimulation," explains Dr. Bahne Bahners, first author of the study, who works at Düsseldorf University Hospital. "By stimulating regions that are connected to the identified network, we will probably be able to adjust DBS settings more precisely in the future, especially in patients who have not yet benefited optimally from deep brain stimulation."

The findings could therefore provide a foundation for making deep brain stimulation more precisely tailored to an individual patient's brain network, particularly when existing DBS settings do not provide the desired level of symptom relief.

Researchers now plan to investigate more directly how deep brain stimulation causes changes within brain networks. Studies examining these causal effects are currently underway.

The study was largely funded by the Professor Klaus Thiemann Foundation.

Materials provided by University of Cologne. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9573. A Van Gogh hidden away for over 50 years and a vibrant Cezanne harlequin: our pick of the November auctions

Vincent van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (blossoming chestnut trees) during the final weeks of his life, having just moved to the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise after spending the previous year in a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Initially he took to painting with a renewed optimism at his surroundings and work. The painting at hand depicts flowering chestnut trees blooming into a blue sky, with women passing through with parasols and Japanese-inspired dress. Châtaigniers en fleurs is expected to fetch in the region of $180m, Sotheby’s says. The artist’s current record at auction is $117.2m, set by Christie’s New York in November 2022 during the Paul Allen sale with Verger avec cyprès (orchard with cypresses, 1888). Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been seen in public since entering the Argentinian Blaquier-Arrieta collection in 1975.

Arlequin is a rare appearance on the market of one of Paul Cezanne’s paintings from his harlequin series, modelled on his son, Paul, and inspired by Mardi Gras parades from the artist’s childhood in Aix-en-Provence, France. It is one of only four such examples, according to Sotheby’s. When the painting was unveiled at Sotheby’s in London, it was the first time it had been seen in public since 1975, when it was acquired by the sugar magnates Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Before it entered their collection in Argentina, it belonged to legendary dealers like Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg. It also hung for two decades at Merton Hall in Cambridge, the then-family home of the British branch of the Rothschild family. Another version of the painting is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. If it exceeds its estimate, Arlequin could set an artist record at auction. The most valuable Cezanne to sell at auction was a view of his beloved Sainte-Victoire mountain, for $137.79m, at Christie’s New York in 2022 during the sale of Paul Allen’s collection.

Man Ray’s Le Baiser (the kiss) comes from the collection of Roger Therond, the journalist and longtime editor of Paris Match, whose holdings included photographs by some of the leading artists of inter-war Paris. Therond was particularly drawn to Man Ray, whom he nicknamed “the Frenzied One”. In Le Baiser, two figures are captured in ambiguous poses, leaving the relationship between the two sitters deliberately unclear. According to Christie’s, Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph from a distance and imagine different possibilities and circumstances for the subjects. The sitter on the left side is the American photographer Lee Miller, who began her career as a fashion model and later worked as a correspondent for Vogue during the Second World War. Miller was one of the first journalists to arrive at the Dachau concentration camp after its liberation in 1945, and recorded some of the most haunting photographic evidence of the Holocaust. She famously posed for a photo while bathing in Adolf Hitler’s personal bathtub at his Munich apartment.

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”, which has been hidden away for over 60 years, is being sold by Sotheby's for the Blaquier-Arrieta family of Argentina

#9572. A stress hormone may help the brain repair itself

When laboratory mice experience brain damage, e.g., from an injection, Jan Deussing repeatedly notices the same response. A particular group of cells appears and becomes active around the damaged area. Although Deussing, a research group leader and experienced neurobiologist, had observed the phenomenon many times, he did not know exactly what type of cells were involved.

The mystery became an ideal research question for a master's student. Clemens Ries, who had recently joined the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry for an internship as he approached the end of his biology degree, took on the challenge.

Using a mouse model, Ries systematically tested markers for all known cell types. Only one produced a response: the marker for oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs).

These precursor cells can mature into oligodendrocytes, which produce the myelin sheath surrounding axons. Axons are extensions of nerve cells that allow neurons to communicate with one another. Myelin acts much like the insulating material around an electrical cable. It supports efficient information transmission along axons and also helps supply them with nutrients, making it vital to healthy brain function.

Damage to myelin can have serious consequences. In autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS), the protective coating breaks down. Physical injuries can also harm myelin, and in severe cases, the resulting damage can lead to the death of entire neurons. Restoring myelin around affected axons is therefore an important part of the brain's response to injury.

A Surprising Stress Hormone Appears After Injury

Ries initially studied the newly identified cells for his master's thesis. "The topic remained so exciting that it became my doctoral thesis," says the biologist.

His subsequent research showed that these precursor cells multiply dramatically around the edges of brain wounds. Most then continue to mature, eventually becoming oligodendrocytes capable of producing new myelin.

But Ries and Deussing also uncovered something that had not been known before. Near the damaged tissue, about one third of the OPCs activate corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), a hormone that plays a central role in regulating the body's stress response. Researchers had not previously known that OPCs could produce neuropeptides such as CRH. The findings have now been published in the renowned journal Cell Reports.

The CRH response begins remarkably quickly. Production can be detected within just a few hours after an injury, but it shuts down again after roughly three days. This short and rapid burst suggests that CRH has an important function during the earliest stages of the healing response.

CRH Helps Control the Timing of Myelin Repair

One of the two known receptors for CRH also appears to be central to this process. CRH receptor 1 is present on a different population of OPCs and allows those cells to respond to the CRH that has been released.

When CRHR1 is absent, OPCs multiply more rapidly after an injury. That initial increase, however, does not translate into better repair. Ultimately, fewer mature oligodendrocytes are produced and remain.

The findings indicate that CRH helps regulate the timing of OPC maturation. That timing appears to be essential for producing enough mature oligodendrocytes to properly restore the damaged myelin sheath.

The Same System Shapes the Developing Brain

OPCs are not only important after injury. They also have a major role in building myelin as the brain matures. Much of this myelination takes place after birth and continues until young adulthood.

Because CRH receptor 1 is found on OPCs even when no injury is present, Ries and Deussing began to wonder whether the receptor might also influence myelination during normal brain development. Working with other researchers, they examined myelin formation in additional mouse models using several different methods.

They found that mice lacking CRH receptor 1 produced more OPCs during the early stages of development. Those changes did not disappear with age. Instead, they had lasting effects on the structure of the brain.

In adult brains, the researchers detected changes in myelination that could be traced to thicker myelin sheaths, particularly around thin axons. The results suggest that CRH receptor 1 on OPCs plays an important role not only in repairing myelin after injury, but also in regulating how myelin develops in the first place.

Where Does CRH Come From During Development?

Following an injury, OPCs themselves respond by producing and releasing CRH. Brain development raises a different question: where does the stress hormone come from when the brain is maturing normally?

The scientists propose that neurons may provide the answer. Their hypothesis is that developing neurons release CRH, which then influences both the multiplication of OPCs and their maturation into oligodendrocytes that produce myelin.

A Possible Connection to Depression and Stress

Neurons are already known to release CRH, particularly during stressful conditions. Stress experienced during early childhood development is also recognized as a risk factor for psychiatric disorders.

The new results therefore raise the possibility that the CRH system operating in OPCs could have broader implications for mental health.

"Our current findings suggest that in stress-associated psychiatric disorders such as depression, the CRH system in OPCs may play a greater role than previously known," Deussing speculates.

If future research confirms and expands on that connection, understanding how CRH signaling affects OPCs, myelin formation, and brain development could eventually point toward completely new therapeutic approaches.

#9571. How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

#9570. In a friends-with-benefits relationship (FWB)? 6 tips to know

A friendship has turned physical, but everything else seems to be staying the same. You grab dinner, send memes, and share inside jokes, all with the understanding that it’s just casual. And yet, you can’t help but wonder where things are headed.

Friends-with-benefits relationships sit in the gray area between friendship and romance. These arrangements work out well for some people, but for others, they slowly become a source of anxiety or hurt.

Whether you're already in one or just curious what you'd be signing up for, here's a closer look at what a friends-with-benefits relationship involves — the risks and the rewards, plus how to navigate one with grace and self-awareness.

A friends-with-benefits relationship (often shortened to FWB) is when two friends are also physically involved with each other, without the commitment or expectations that come with a romantic partnership. There's no exclusivity agreement (unless discussed), no defined future together, and usually none of the relationship milestones that come with dating.

The idea is that the friendship stays intact while you enjoy the physical side of a relationship, no strings attached. It may sound straightforward, but in practice, it usually takes more communication and honesty than people expect going in.

Every FWB relationship looks different. Some see each other regularly, while others keep it more sporadic. What they generally have in common is a mutual understanding that neither person is looking for something more serious.

Not sure if you’re in one? Here are some signs that point toward a FWB dynamic:

You skip the things typical couples do, like meeting each other's families or planning trips together.

You haven’t talked about exclusivity or where the relationship is headed.

You call each other “friends” when describing your situation to others.

You’re dating, or open to dating, other people.

The relationship stays undefined, and one or both of you is comfortable keeping it that way.

Like any relationship structure, being friends with benefits has its upsides and its risks. If you're deciding whether to start a FWB relationship, this list is a good gut check for whether the upsides outweigh the risks for you.

Physical intimacy without the pressure of commitment

Closeness and companionship that come from an existing friendship

More freedom to focus on other priorities, like your career, personal growth, or social life

Low-stakes exploration if you’re not ready for something serious

Clarity about what you want (or don’t want) from relationships

One-sided feelings that go unnoticed or unspoken

Ambiguity about what the relationship actually is, even as time passes

Jealousy, especially if one of you starts dating someone else

Damage to the friendship if it ends badly

Lack of communication about needs due to unclear expectations

FWB relationships don't come with a rulebook — but there are common threads among the ones that work: honesty, self-awareness, and ongoing communication. These tips follow those threads.

FWB tension often comes from mismatched expectations that were never discussed. Before you get physically involved—or as soon as possible if you already are—have an open conversation about what you both want.

Get clear about what “casual” means to each of you, and make sure you're both comfortable with it. Talking through this early beats untangling confusion later.

💙 For more guidance, here’s how to set healthy boundaries in relationships.

Unless you've agreed otherwise, friends-with-benefits arrangements are usually non-exclusive, meaning either of you could be dating or getting involved with someone else. It's worth discussing up front how you'll handle that — will you tell each other when someone new is in the picture?

Your feelings about a FWB setup might shift over time. Take a moment every so often to check in on how you're feeling about the situation.

A few minutes of reflection, or a short meditation, can help you notice any uncomfortable feelings you've been avoiding.

💙 Try Checking In With Yourself with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

Without active effort, the friendship side of FWB can slowly fade into the background until only the physical side is left.

Make it a point to spend time together without getting intimate. Ask about different parts of their life. Show up for each other the way you would have before your dynamic changed.

💙 Learn more about Mindful Friendships with Jay Shetty on Calm.

A FWB arrangement that works one month might not work the next. People's feelings and circumstances naturally evolve with time. The key is speaking up when you notice a change, whether it’s on your end or theirs.

This is where these relationships often get complicated. One of you has a change of heart, but stays silent, afraid of disrupting the dynamic or losing the other person.

Being upfront can be uncomfortable, but it’s one of the most respectful things you can do for yourself and your friend.

💙 Press play on Say What You Need to Say with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Any friends-with-benefits relationship could end at some point, and thinking ahead about how you'd handle it can reduce the fallout. Think about whether preserving the friendship matters to you. Either way, expect some awkwardness afterward.

It can be hard to end things with care and honesty, but it does less damage to the friendship than silence or avoidance.

Knowing what to do in a FWB situation matters, but it’s equally important to be aware of what can trip you up.

Don't assume you're on the same page without checking. Shared silence isn't shared understanding.

Don't use the arrangement as a way to stay close to someone you have feelings for. That's a recipe for getting hurt.

Don't ignore your feelings because they feel inconvenient. Feelings that get dismissed tend to resurface louder later.

Don't skip the conversation about seeing other people. Assumptions here can turn this arrangement messy fast.

Don't stay in it if you’re consistently left feeling worse. A casual relationship isn't worth more than your peace of mind.

Don't expect the friendship to survive constant unspoken tension. Even close friendships have limits, and unspoken hurt can gradually erode them.

Friends with benefits means you and your friend are physically intimate without the commitments of a romantic relationship. There's no assumed exclusivity and no defined future — just a dynamic that exists somewhere between friendship and romance.

Friends-with-benefits relationships get complicated when feelings become one-sided. One of you may develop deeper feelings while the other doesn't. It can also get tricky when expectations shift without a conversation, when one of you starts dating someone else, or when the physical side starts overshadowing the friendship.

There's no set timeline for a FWB relationship. Some arrangements last a few months, while others go on for years. How long yours lasts depends on whether you’re both comfortable with it, communication stays open, and your feelings stay compatible over time.

Friends with benefits may be a good idea if you and the other person are aligned on what you’re looking for. It can be a comfortable, low-pressure arrangement, or a source of confusion and hurt if expectations aren't discussed. Open communication and regular self-reflection tend to give the relationship the best shot at working.

Yes, some FWB arrangements do evolve into committed relationships, particularly when both people develop feelings around the same time and are open to more. That said, staying in the arrangement in hopes that it'll turn into something more comes with a risk. You may end up hurt if the other person doesn't feel the same way.

Jealousy is a normal reaction, even in FWB arrangements that are meant to be casual. This happens because intimacy can naturally lead to attachment. If you’re feeling this way, it might be a sign the situation no longer fits what you want.

The best way to end a friends-with-benefits relationship without ruining the friendship is to be direct and honest. Ghosting or avoiding the other person usually does more damage than an open conversation. Be clear about why things have changed, share appreciation for what you had, and give each other some space afterward.

#9568. A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it

Ursula Quitterer calls it "Compound 10," a chemical substance developed by her research team that could potentially slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

Quitterer, Professor of Molecular Pharmacology at ETH Zurich, has so far tested the experimental treatment in mice. The results were encouraging. The nerve cell death typically associated with dementia slowed significantly, and the treated animals lived longer.

The work behind the compound began nearly 20 years ago, when Quitterer received brain tissue samples from patients treated by a doctor and colleague at Ain Shams University Hospital in Cairo. The tissue had been removed during tumor surgery from people with dementia as well as non-dementia patients.

Quitterer used those samples to investigate an enzyme called GRK2, which has long been a major focus of her research.

GRK2 plays an important regulatory role in many human cells. It helps cells respond appropriately to signals, stress, and strain. The enzyme is active in organs including the heart and the brain, where it helps support normal nerve cell function.

By analyzing the Cairo tissue samples at the molecular level and conducting experiments in mice, Quitterer and her colleagues uncovered evidence that GRK2 plays an important role in dementia. Their findings were recently published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

GRK2 exists in cells in two forms. One is normal and functional, while the other has been inactivated by cellular metabolism.

Quitterer's team found unusually large amounts of the inactive form in brain tissue from people with dementia. The researchers observed the same pattern in mice, specifically in a mouse model for Alzheimer's disease.

They also discovered that inactive GRK2 can clump together inside brain cells during dementia. These aggregates collect on mitochondria (the "powerhouses" of the cells), where they can interfere with normal function and cause damage.

"The GRK2 aggregates block the pores of the mitochondria, reducing the amount of energy they can supply and leading to a situation of stress inside the cells," Quitterer explains.

The mouse experiments revealed another important effect. Inactive GRK2 appeared to increase production of amyloid beta, a protein fragment that is considered a main cause of Alzheimer's.

That process can then feed back on itself. Amyloid beta places additional stress on nerve cells, and that stress encourages the formation of more inactive GRK2 and more GRK2 aggregates. The result is a vicious circle that can contribute to the progression of dementia.

To interrupt this process, Quitterer and her colleagues created several chemical compounds and tested them in cell cultures and mice.

Compound 10 stood out as particularly effective. It prevented GRK2 molecules from forming aggregates, which allowed mitochondria to function better. The researchers also saw less amyloid beta accumulating in cells, while nerve cells were better able to maintain their function and avoid dying.

The effects were not limited to the brain.

In mice, compound 10 also had a positive effect on heart function and aging processes. One visible example was that older animals developed fewer grey hairs.

The broader effects of compound 10 suggest that interfering with GRK2 aggregation may influence more than Alzheimer's related processes.

In addition to protecting nerve cells and supporting mitochondrial function, the compound appeared to benefit the heart and affect some signs of aging in the mice.

These findings remain preclinical, however. Compound 10 has not yet been developed into a treatment for people.

The researchers have applied for a patent covering compound 10, and the basic research phase has now been completed.

"It took so long simply because everything takes so long in Alzheimer's research," explains Quitterer.

Because Alzheimer's is an age-related disease, the team needed to conduct experiments using older animals. In mice, that means working with animals that are about one and a half to two years old.

Each experiment can also require roughly one and a half to two years before researchers have enough information to draw conclusions and design the next study.

"It's all a great deal slower than in cancer research, for example."

Quitterer and ETH Zurich are now searching for a company interested in helping move the compound toward the next stages of drug development.

A Different Approach to Treating Alzheimer's

"Alzheimer's is a very complex disease," says Quitterer.

Existing medications do not cure Alzheimer's. At best, they can delay its progression by several months.

"That's why it's so important that we've now identified a new target protein in the form of GRK2, as well as an active ingredient that operates via GRK2 and therefore via a different mechanism than existing Alzheimer's drugs."

Because compound 10 acts through a different biological pathway, the researchers believe it could potentially complement existing treatments rather than replace them.

Using compound 10 alongside other medications may one day help improve quality of life for people with Alzheimer's disease.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9566. What is a circadian rhythm disorder? Plus, 6 ways to treat it

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re tired when you should be awake, or wired when you should be asleep. Whether it’s 2am and you’re staring at the ceiling, your body still hasn’t recovered from that red-eye flight, or the night shift is taking its toll, the struggle is the same: your internal clock and your life are pulling in opposite directions.

These are circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs), and they happen when your body's sleep-wake cycle doesn't match your daily schedule. And they're more common than you'd think — often mistaken for stress or brushed off as one more thing to deal with once life slows down.

The good news is that CRSDs are medically recognized and treatable. Below, we’ll cover the different types, why they happen, and how to get your sleep back on track.

Your body has an internal clock—the circadian rhythm—that regulates when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. It runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle, shaped by external cues like light, temperature, and meal timing.

A circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) occurs when your internal clock consistently falls out of sync with your environment, social schedule, or desired sleep times.

There are several distinct types of circadian rhythm sleep disorders:

Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD): Sleep comes much later than usual (often in the early hours of the morning) followed by a struggle to wake up on time.

Advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD): Sleep arrives early in the evening, and waking happens in the early hours of the morning — the reverse of DSPD.

Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder: Sleep and wake times drift later or earlier each day instead of settling into a 24-hour rhythm. This pattern is most common in people who are blind.

Irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder: Sleep is broken into several short stretches across the day and night, without a clear pattern.

Shift work disorder: Night or rotating shift schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep timing.

Jet lag disorder: A temporary misalignment between the body’s internal clock and local time after crossing time zones.

Symptoms vary based on the type of CRSD, but the core issue is the same: sleep happens at the wrong time.

trouble falling asleep at a normal bedtime

difficulty waking up in the morning, or waking too early

mood changes, including irritability, anxiety, or low mood

Circadian rhythm sleep disorders often stem from multiple factors at once, ranging from lifestyle and environment to biology.

Light exposure: Light entering your eyes is the strongest external cue for your internal clock to stay in sync with the outside world. Too much bright light at night, like from screens, or too little natural light in the morning can push your clock in the wrong direction.

Genetics: Your genes can set your natural sleep timing earlier or later than average. Certain gene variants have been linked to differences in circadian timing, which may explain a lifelong tendency toward being a night owl or an early riser.

Age: Your sleep timing usually changes with age. Teenagers drift toward later sleep and wake times, while older adults often feel tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier as a result.

Shift work and irregular schedules: Night or rotating shifts keep you awake when your body expects to be asleep. Irregular eating and exercise can add to that disruption.

Neurological conditions: Conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or a history of traumatic brain injury are tied to a higher risk of circadian disruption, including fragmented or irregular sleep. Researchers are still working out whether disrupted rhythms are a cause, an early sign, or both.

Blindness: Without light entering the eyes, the brain's clock loses its main external cue for staying aligned with a 24-hour day.

No matter which type of CRSD you're dealing with, you can get your internal clock back on track. Here's what works, and how to find the right approach for you.

In the morning: Bright daylight early in the day helps advance your clock, which is especially useful for delayed sleep phase disorder. During darker months, using a bright light therapy box (10,000 lux) for 20–30 minutes after waking can substitute for sunlight. If you have any eye conditions, it's a good idea to check with a doctor before starting.

In the evening: Reduce bright light 2–3 hours before bed to ease your body into sleep mode. Screens and overhead lighting can suppress melatonin production, while dimmer, warmer light helps your body settle down.

Traveling across time zones? The strategy for beating jet lag with light depends on which direction you're flying. Seek bright light in the new morning and avoid it in the new evening when flying east. Do the reverse when flying west. A day or two of light timing can speed up your adjustment.

💙 Pair your morning light with a Morning Meditation from the Daily Calm.

One of the most effective ways to steady your circadian rhythm is to maintain a regular sleep schedule. Wake up at the same time every day—even on weekends—to give your body a consistent cue to work with. It may feel hard at first, but with consistency, your body naturally adjusts to the rhythm.

Working nights or rotating shifts? "Consistent" doesn't have to mean conventional. Try anchoring your sleep to the same block of hours on workdays, and limiting how far you drift on days off.

💙 Build a sleep routine with Making Progress from the 7 Days of Sleep series on Calm.

Chronotherapy involves slowly adjusting your sleep and wake times in one direction, a little each day, until you reach your target schedule.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? This might mean going to bed a few hours later each day (moving all the way around the clock) until you land on your desired bedtime. It's a demanding process, and there's some risk of your schedule drifting further off track, so it's best done under a sleep specialist's guidance rather than on your own.

A sleep specialist can help tailor chronotherapy to your specific pattern.

Sleep difficulties often come with anxiety about sleep itself, which can make it harder to fall asleep. Mindfulness practices can help calm your racing mind and relieve that anxiety. Even a few minutes of mindful breathing or a short guided meditation can quiet your mind enough to help you drift off.

💙 Try this Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain produces, and its levels naturally rise in the evening — signaling to your body that sleep time is approaching. Think of a melatonin supplement as a timing tool rather than a sedative that will help you fall asleep on the spot.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? Take a low dose (around 0.5–3 mg) three hours before your desired bedtime to help adjust your clock gradually. A doctor or sleep specialist can advise on the right amount for your situation.

Traveling across time zones? Melatonin taken around your target bedtime (about an hour before) in the new time zone is a well-supported way to adjust to jet lag faster.

💙 Discover the best time to take melatonin for restful sleep.

For persistent or severe circadian rhythm sleep disorders, professional support can make a real difference. A sleep specialist may recommend a formal evaluation, actigraphy (a wrist sensor that tracks sleep-wake patterns over time), or a combination of treatments.

Struggling with non-24-hour or irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder? These patterns respond less predictably to light and schedule changes on their own. A sleep specialist can build a plan around your specific pattern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is also sometimes paired with circadian-focused treatments. It’s a structured therapy that targets the thoughts and habits keeping you awake.

Several everyday habits can throw off your circadian rhythm, including irregular sleep schedules, shift work, jet lag, too much screen use at night, and inconsistent light exposure. Stress, alcohol, caffeine, and some medications can also throw off your body's timing.

Some circadian rhythm sleep disorders can go away on their own, but it depends on the type you're dealing with. Jet lag usually clears up within a few days as your body adjusts to a new time zone. But most chronic circadian rhythm sleep disorders don't resolve without changes to your sleep schedule, light exposure, or daily habits. The sooner you start addressing it, the more manageable the shift becomes.

Not quite, though circadian rhythm sleep disorder and insomnia can feel similar. Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep, no matter the time of day. A circadian rhythm sleep disorder is sleep happening at the wrong time. Someone with delayed sleep phase disorder, for example, might sleep just fine from 3am to 11am, instead of a more typical schedule.

The time it takes to reset your circadian rhythm depends on how far your body clock has shifted. Jet lag typically settles within a few days, but a significantly delayed or advanced sleep schedule can take several weeks of consistent habit changes to correct. Light therapy and melatonin can speed the process along, but there's no quick fix.

Melatonin can help with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, but the timing matters. For delayed sleep phase disorder, a low dose taken several hours before your target bedtime can help shift your clock gradually. For jet lag, taking it closer to your target bedtime tends to work better. A doctor or sleep specialist can help you figure out the right dose and timing for your situation.

If your sleep schedule has been getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life—and adjusting your habits hasn’t helped—it's worth reaching out to a doctor or sleep specialist. They can assess whether you have a circadian rhythm sleep disorder and recommend a treatment plan.

💙 Learn more about the 7 most common sleep disorders.

In many cases, you can fix your circadian rhythm naturally. Focus on getting bright light in the morning and keeping consistent sleep and wake times. For milder patterns, these changes alone can make a noticeable difference, though more serious cases may need extra support.

#9565. Fifth generation Indian weaver launches luxury cashmere brand

Kadri’s ‘Triangle Twill’ two-tone, hand-painted scarves are 100% cashmere and retail for $400 each. Designs for the brand’s inaugural range were created in a studio in Paris Mickaël Llorca

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

Mujtaba Kadri’s family has produced cashmere for five generations and his atelier in Srinagar, the largest city in Kashmir, is just 50m away from where his great-grandfather had his own. “I’ve been involved since I was a child,” Kadri says. His spinners and weavers are still based exclusively in Srinagar, mostly women working from home. Hand spinning creates a slightly uneven texture in the fibre, which leaves tiny air pockets once it is woven. It is this that makes the fabric both very light and incredibly warm.

Kadri studied at university in Mumbai but returned immediately to his home city, albeit with a more international outlook. “Our cashmere is the finest quality, which means its micron count is always below 14.5,” Kadri says. “I knew it had potential in foreign markets.” He went on to work with Carolina Herrera, Oscar de la Renta and Marni, making custom-ordered textiles. Later, he met Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, and collaborated closely with their label, The Row, when they launched their home line.

He is now launching the Kadri brand, using his own name, via the online retailer Net A Porter. On sale will be scarves, blankets and other home and fashion accessories. “I’ve wanted to do this for a long time,” he says. Designs are developed in a small Paris studio where the creative team includes colour specialist Maeva Elfassi. “Colour can be the element that cashmere brands get wrong,” Kadri says.

Hand-woven cashmere is expensive due to the rare raw materials, from a special breed of Changthangi goats, and its time-consuming production. A shawl, which sells for $1,000, will go through 12 processes, undertaken by a number of artisans, and takes 40 days to make. “It really is slow fashion,” Kadri says. But more importantly, for him, it is a way to sustain a community where weaving has always been a way of life.

#9564. A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure

Certain imagery-based psychotherapy techniques may help reduce fear of failure connected to painful childhood experiences, according to research from scientists at SWPS University and the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology. The findings were published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

Difficult experiences early in life, including criticism, neglect, or severe reactions from caregivers, can influence emotional well-being and quality of life years later. How adults respond when a child makes a mistake may be especially important in shaping future patterns of thought and emotion. In some cases, those experiences can contribute to a fear of failure rooted in the belief that mistakes make a person less worthy in the eyes of others.

Researchers from the Poznań-based Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University, and the Laboratory of Brain Imaging at the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology in Warsaw set out to determine whether imagery-based psychotherapy could reduce the ongoing effects of these painful memories on everyday life.

Testing Whether Memory Work Can Create Lasting Change

The randomized, controlled clinical trial included 180 young adults (between 18 and 35 years of age) who experienced fear of failure. During a two-week period, participants took part in four therapy sessions focused on difficult childhood memories involving criticism.

One group used the Imagery Exposure (IE) technique. Participants were asked to recall situations that had triggered fear or anxiety (the active control group).

A second group received Imagery Rescripting (ImRs), a technique designed to change the way a memory unfolds in the imagination. Participants brought a distressing experience to mind and then imagined a "defender" (e.g., a therapist) entering the scene, confronting the person delivering the criticism, and offering support to the child.

The third group used the same therapeutic approach, but with a 10-minute delay procedure (ImRs-DSR). Researchers designed this delay to interfere with the memory trace associated with the critical experience, potentially strengthening the intervention's effects.

Participants completed questionnaires and interviews, while researchers also tracked physiological measures. Follow-up assessments took place three and six months later.

All of the imagery-based approaches produced a significant and lasting reduction in fear of failure. Participants also reported lower levels of negative emotions, including sadness and guilt.

Their bodies appeared to respond differently as well. Physiological reactions to memories of criticism decreased, indicating that recalling distressing experiences no longer triggered the same level of intense stress. These improvements remained evident during follow-ups at three and six months, suggesting that the psychological effects were stable over time.

"The study shows that it is possible to reduce the intensity of negative emotions and arousal associated with memories of childhood criticism. Properly selected techniques can influence how these memories are experienced, making them less burdensome," says study co-author Julia Bączek, a psychologist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.

The researchers found that imagery rescripting worked especially well when it produced a moment of surprise. They linked this effect to prediction error, which occurs when there is a mismatch between what someone expects and what actually happens.

That unexpected difference may help loosen established emotional patterns and make it easier for the mind to replace old, painful responses with new ones.

"We have shown that a crucial part of imagery-based therapy is creating a discrepancy between what the patient expects and what actually happens in the new memory. It is this surprise that paves the way for a lasting therapeutic change," says study co-author Stanisław Karkosz, a cognitive scientist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.

Painful Memories Do Not Have to Stay Emotionally Fixed

The findings suggest that imagery-based techniques can change how people respond to current challenges by allowing them to "write" new, safe endings to painful experiences from the past.

The results also indicate that difficult memories (including those related to failure) do not necessarily have to be experienced in the same emotional way forever. Julia Bączek emphasizes that past experiences can be processed differently over time, rather than remaining fixed and unchangeable.

#9563. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9561. Body doubling: what it is, how it works, and tips to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

If you’ve ever opened your laptop to begin your workday from home or checked your mountain of a to-do list and felt zero motivation to tackle it, you’re in good company. On days that you just can’t find the energy or focus to get started, it can help to have a little boost of accountability.

Body doubling, a phrase that means working alongside another person, has gained popularity over the years and is especially popular among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Body doubling (either in person or virtually) is said to help motivate people to stay focused and accountable for the tasks at hand. And while it isn’t a formal treatment or backed by robust clinical research, plenty of people have spoken to its effectiveness.

So, what does body doubling involve, and why do so many people swear by it? More importantly, will it work for you? Pull up a seat and let’s explore what you need to know about the technique, plus a few simple ways to try it out for yourself.

Body doubling is the practice of working alongside another person to stay focused and complete a task, either in the same space or virtually. According to the ADDA, the term “body doubling” was coined in the late 1990s by ADHD coach Linda Anderson.

The rationale behind body doubling is that having someone else present and engaged in their own task can make it easier to start and stay on track with yours. To be clear, there’s no coaching or collaboration involved. You’re just working next to each other, because a shared presence can create a sense of structure and accountability.

If you sit at your kitchen table while your roommate does homework, join a silent Zoom session where everyone works on their own projects, or even fold laundry while a friend cleans their space on FaceTime, those are all examples of body doubling.

Many people feel that body doubling helps them break through procrastination and maintain momentum,  especially during overwhelming tasks.

Getting started: Sometimes the hardest part is just beginning. Having someone else nearby can help create a sense of gentle urgency.

Staying on task: When another person is focused, it can be easier for you to stay engaged with your own work.

Feeling less isolated: This practice can reduce the emotional friction that builds when you’re feeling alone in your head.

Creating structure: Knowing someone will be present at a specific time gives your day a natural rhythm. Plus, it can add a layer of accountability.

This technique has gained popularity within the ADHD community. While it’s important to note that this isn’t a clinically recommended treatment—and there’s limited research to support it—many people with ADHD do say that it helps them function more consistently. The idea is that having someone nearby provides external structure and co-regulation.

When your executive functioning is impaired, simple tasks can feel overwhelming. But body doubling creates a soft sense of accountability, which can make it easier to begin and stay engaged in tasks.

With that said, some people find it distracting or feel pressure to “perform,” especially if their partner’s energy doesn’t match theirs. Additionally, if your body double doesn’t understand ADHD, their presence can sometimes feel more frustrating than supportive.

If you’re navigating ADHD, body doubling could be another great tool to add to your toolkit. But only if it feels natural to you.

Disclaimer: Please note that body doubling isn’t a substitute for medication or therapy for people with ADHD.

If you find it hard to begin or stay engaged with tasks, body doubling could be the flexible tool you need. To get started, look for someone who matches your energy and who also makes you feel comfortable.

Here are nine ways you can mindfully add body doubling into your life.

If you’re new to body doubling, try it during something that feels manageable, like folding laundry or organizing your desk. This can give you space to experiment without the pressure of a high-stakes deadline or an environment that isn’t familiar to you, like a coworking space or coffee shop.

Have a quick conversation about what you both want. Ask the other person if you’ll talk, stay silent, or check in at the end.

Clear expectations help make the experience smooth and more supportive.

💙 Stay on the same page with your coworking partner with guidance from Jay Shetty’s Expectations.

Working alongside others in total silence can be helpful for concentrating and removing social pressure, while still giving you the benefits of shared presence.

Try scheduling a Zoom session where you say hello, then mute yourselves and work independently. You could also start a silent group video call with coworkers and only use the chat to check in.

If real-time body doubling feels overwhelming or isn’t accessible, consider searching for helpful videos on YouTube or TikTok.

Search for “study with me” or “body doubling,” and you’ll find creators who film themselves doing everyday tasks. By watching someone else stay focused, it may help you do the same.

Whether it’s a weekly Sunday cleaning hour with a friend or a daily Zoom session at 9am, a recurring slot can build structure into your routine. This can be especially helpful if you struggle with executive function challenges.

Related read: Meditation for ADHD: 9 tips and techniques

You and your body double don’t need to be doing the same thing. One of you could be writing emails while the other is meal prepping or baking a cake.

What matters most is that the energy feels aligned, focused, and respectful.

Related read: How to focus better: 8 tips to improve concentration

Make whatever task you’re doing as manageable as possible. Choose a specific task to start with, and try doing it for 15–30 minutes at first.

This reduces overwhelm and helps give you a clear finish line.

Some people feel vulnerable doing tasks in front of others, especially ones tied to shame or executive dysfunction.

So, choose a body double who won’t judge or try to fix you.

💙 Learn how to build relationships with people you trust during this Mindful Friendships session with Jay Shetty.

If you prefer asynchronous support, text a friend when you start a task and again when you finish. On the flip side, if you’re more motivated in groups, explore coworking in community accountability spaces.

Remember, there’s no one right way to body double. The key is to experiment and adjust based on what feels good to you.

Yes. Body doubling only needs one other person who is working at the same time as you. They can be in the room or on a video call. They don’t need to share your task or give you feedback.

Whether it works varies from person to person. Research on body doubling is limited, and many reports come from people who have tried it. Start with one short session and notice if it’s easier to begin and stay on task.

Body doubling works by providing subtle social accountability and structure. When another person is present, your brain registers the shift in environment. This presence can make it easier for you to start a task or stay with it.

And the accountability can be enough to kickstart momentum, especially if you’re someone who tends to overthink or avoid certain tasks.

It can. Procrastination often stems from overwhelm, perfectionism, and decision fatigue. But body doubling can add a sense of time and presence. You can see that there’s someone else there doing their own thing. And, as a result, it can become a little easier for you to start doing your own thing.

It allows the pressure of the task to lift, even though it may still feel hard.

There can be cons of body doubling. Some people find it distracting, especially if the other person wants to talk and you don’t. Additionally, if you have social anxiety or a history of trauma, being observed might make you feel emotionally charged.

In general, this practice isn’t for everyone. If you’re curious, check in with yourself. Ask if it’s something that would feel supportive and safe. If not, then it’s okay to step back and try a different format.

Anyone can try body doubling. While the term does have roots in ADHD communities, the technique can be applied to anyone. If you struggle with focus or motivation, this practice might be the thing for you.

Plus, if you’ve ever gotten more done in a coffee shop than at home, or felt a boost from working silently next to a friend, you’ve already experienced a version of body doubling.

You don’t need someone in the same room to try body doubling. Virtual options can be just as effective. You could join a coworking session on Zoom or even stream a “study with me” video in the background.

That being said, if you’d rather keep it low-contact, text a friend when you’re about to start a task. Then text them again when you finish. The key isn’t the format; it’s the feeling of shared effort and accountability. So, do whatever feels right to you.

#9560. Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes

The human brain is continuously processing enormous amounts of information. Even something as familiar as driving requires several mental tasks at once. The brain must remember the route, recall how to control the vehicle, and respond to unexpected developments such as a road closure or shifting traffic conditions.

A brain network known as the frontoparietal cortex plays a major role in managing this flow of information. It receives signals from throughout the brain, determines which information is most important, and helps coordinate the appropriate response.

New research from the University of Iowa offers a more detailed look at how this system works when people face uncertainty while making decisions. The findings show how the frontoparietal cortex helps organize information and coordinate responses involving both the brain and the body.

University of Iowa researchers have provided new insight into the brain's information hub, known as the frontoparietal cortex. In this illustration, colored areas identify frontoparietal regions that track uncertainty as participants encounter changes in associations they had previously learned. Image courtesy of Kai Hwang lab, University of Iowa.

Using experiments that combined computational modeling with brain imaging, the researchers found that the frontoparietal cortex does not communicate with the rest of the brain in a fixed way. Instead, its connections shift according to the type of information required during different stages of a decision.

The results could help guide future investigations into neurological and psychiatric conditions in which this information exchange may function differently, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and schizophrenia.

"Our study shows in more detail how the frontoparietal cortex operates -- what kind of information it extracts from other systems and how it uses its connectivity pattern to integrate information that is coming in from different areas of the brain," says Kai Hwang, associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences and the study's corresponding author. "That's the main contribution."

Scientists have long recognized the frontoparietal cortex as an important part of decision making. Its role resembles that of an air traffic controller overseeing a crowded airport. It continually receives information from other brain regions, but it does more than simply collect those signals. Depending on the situation, it filters out some information while giving greater attention to signals that are more relevant.

Building a Big Picture From Incomplete Information

In a study published in 2025, Hwang and his colleagues found that the frontoparietal cortex develops an ongoing high-level summary of information arriving from elsewhere in the brain. It evaluates incoming signals, including information that may be incomplete or uncertain, combines them into a more useful overall representation, and then helps direct other brain regions toward an appropriate response.

"It's like where other areas of the brain don't have all the information, so they send what they have to the frontoparietal cortex for guidance," Hwang explains.

The new research extended those findings by examining how adaptable the frontoparietal cortex is. Specifically, the scientists wanted to understand how its interactions with other brain regions change as the demands of a problem or situation change.

To investigate this, the team recruited 38 participants between ages 18 and 35. Participants learned connections between different combinations of colors, faces, and scenes and particular responses. Those responses included pressing a button using either the index or middle finger on either hand.

The researchers later altered the learned pairings. Participants therefore had to recognize that the associations had changed, learn the new ones, and respond with the correct button using the appropriate hand and finger.

Changing the instructions introduced uncertainty into the task. That allowed the researchers to observe how the frontoparietal cortex changed its connections with other brain systems as participants tried to determine what had happened.

"If they always get it right, they know they've made the correct association, but once they start doing it wrong, they will have to guess, 'Oh, did the context change, or did I not see the color clearly?' That creates uncertainty," Hwang says.

The team combined behavioral data from the experiments with functional MRI scans. Using those results, the researchers developed a computational model that separated signals coming from different areas of the brain and revealed how the frontoparietal cortex brought that information together.

"Rather than simply becoming more active during difficult tasks, we observed how this network dynamically changes how it communicates with other brain regions depending on what information is needed at each stage of a decision," Hwang says.

The results suggest that challenging decisions are not handled simply by increasing activity within this network. Instead, the frontoparietal cortex appears to adjust which brain regions it communicates with according to the information needed at that particular moment.

Possible Links to ADHD and Other Disorders

The findings could eventually contribute to research on psychiatric disorders that make it harder for people to adjust their behavior when circumstances change. Examples can include speaking too loudly in a library or struggling to control impulses, difficulties that can occur with ADHD.

"These are situations where people struggle with regulating their behavior. That, to me, is an integration problem. If that integration function is not working properly, then that could very likely mean they didn't use the right context to regulate their behavior," Hwang says.

Stephanie Leach, a sixth-year graduate student in Hwang's lab, contributed to the design of the project, led the experiments conducted with participants, and co-led preparation of the manuscript.

"Having the opportunity to conduct this research has been especially rewarding because it has allowed me to contribute to answering questions about the most fascinating, mysterious, and complex system we know -- the human brain," says Leach, who is the study's first author.

The study, "Frontoparietal hub connectivity integrates information from multiple sources," was published in the Journal of Neuroscience.

Other contributors include Jiefeng Jiang, who led the computational modeling, and Shannon Stokes. Both are members of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

Funding for the research came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the Iowa Neuroscience Institute.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
